newsitem.title: PERU: Japan ambassador's home in Peru attacked by gunmen.
newsitem.headline: Japan ambassador's home in Peru attacked by gunmen.

text.p: About 20 leftist guerrillas armed with automatic weapons and grenade launchers stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima on Tuesday and held hostage about 40 people attending a reception, officials and eyewitnesses said.
Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki in an interview with local radio from within the residency said: "For the moment there are no injuries."
"I cannot speak with liberty. For the moment the firing of the police is more dangerous," he said.
Witnesses said they heard shots exchanged between the gunmen and police guarding the residence but there were no immediate reports of casualties.
The guerrillas were dressed in black and most of the hostages had their hands held high, according to police on buildings around the embassy.

A guerrilla spokesman from inside the ambassador's residence told a local radio station the attack was carried out by the Cuban-inspired Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA), the smaller of two communist-guerrilla groups operating in Peru.
The MRTA guerrilla said the movement wanted to release hostages calmy. "We have tried to get out one group but they (the police) opened fire," he said.
The guerrilla spokesman asked for negotiations to begin with government representatives and asked that the talks be broadcast live.
If the conditions were met, the guerrillas said they would release women and children they were holding hostage. It was not known how many women and children were inside.
Officials on scene said there were no immediate reports of casualties.
Health Minister Marino Costa Bauer said it was not known who was inside the residence when the attack occurred about 8 p.m. EST (0100 GMT Wednesday).
A Reuter photographer from the roof of a nearby building said he saw about 40 hostages and 20 gunmen armed with rifles and grenade launchers.
Local radio said a number of ambassadors, Peruvian businessmen and academics were at the reception when the attack occurred.
At the start of the attack at least six explosions were heard, according to police radio reports.
A Japanese diplomat in Lima said he was caught the attack at the residence and could not leave because of continuing gunfire, a Japanese Foreign Ministry official said in Tokyo.

"I first heard several bombs exploding in front of the official residence of the ambassador," the ministry official quoted Hiroyuki Kimoto, who holds the rank of minister at the embassy, as saying in a call from his mobile phone.
